Sixty-one thousand cars cross this bridge every day.
Nobody sees what holds it up.
To check it, a diver goes down, into water so murky they often work by touch.
Massachusetts has 778 bridges that need this.
And scour is worst in a flood. Exactly when nobody can go in.
Federal rules keep the diver. Sonar can only supplement.
So we asked: what if a robot went first, and divers only went where the map says?
In one day, from scratch, we built it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
A digital twin of this crossing, flown by Ardupilot, the same flight code that runs on real hardware.
Above the water, a drone. Its lidar fires a hundred and twenty-eight laser beams, and turns the bridge into millions of three-D points.
A gimbal camera, and a thermal camera, simulated here, hunt for cracks and damp stone. Floodlights for the underside. R T K G P S for position.
Below, a Blue ROV two. There is no GPS underwater.
So it navigates by sound. A Doppler velocity log pings the riverbed and tracks its own speed. Forty centimetres of drift after sixty metres.
A multibeam sonar sees where the camera sees only silt. Eight thrusters hold it in the current.
The mission. The drone takes the wall.
Under the deck, twelve satellites become seven.
At the waterline it spots damage, and hands the spot to the robot below.
The ROV dives straight to the mark.
Its sonar finds what nobody could see. A missing granite block. A scour pit, timber piles exposed.
Four flagged. Four inspected. One model, above the water and below.
Then the brain, built with Kiro. It finds the defects, cites every one in the report, and waits for an engineer to sign off.
Every finding lands in one dashboard. The three-D map, the camera footage, the G P S track, and a report that Kiro writes itself.
Robot first is twenty to thirty percent cheaper per bridge, by our estimate, on a sixteen-thousand-dollar kit.
By 2028, every state must re-code its scour data. And the pilot money already exists.
Today, it's a simulation. Next, a ten-bridge pilot, checked against divers.
Robot first. Divers only where the map says.
